title: Amyloid-Related Imaging Abnormalities in 2 Phase 3 Studies Evaluating Aducanumab in Patients With Early Alzheimer Disease

one_line: In the EMERGE and ENGAGE phase 3 trials, 41.3% of patients receiving high-dose aducanumab developed amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA), which were mostly asymptomatic and resolved radiographically.
summary: This document reports a secondary analysis of ARIA incidence from the EMERGE and ENGAGE phase 3 randomized clinical trials evaluating aducanumab for early Alzheimer's disease. Among participants receiving the highest dose (10 mg/kg), 41.3% experienced ARIA, with ARIA-edema (ARIA-E) being the most common finding (35.2%). The incidence of ARIA-E was highest during early treatment and among ApoE ε4 carriers. While the majority of ARIA-E cases were asymptomatic and resolved radiographically within 16 weeks, roughly 26% of those with ARIA-E experienced symptoms such as headache, confusion, or dizziness. The findings suggest that while ARIA is a frequent adverse event associated with high-dose aducanumab, it can typically be managed with routine MRI monitoring and targeted dose suspensions.

key_claims.claim: High-dose aducanumab (10 mg/kg) frequently causes ARIA-E, primarily early in the treatment course.
key_claims.evidence: 362 of 1029 patients (35.2%) in the 10-mg/kg group experienced ARIA-E; 72.7% of initial events occurred within the first 8 doses.

key_claims.claim: ApoE ε4 carrier status is a significant risk factor for developing ARIA-E.
key_claims.evidence: Incidence of ARIA-E was 43.0% in ApoE ε4 carriers compared to 20.3% in noncarriers in the 10-mg/kg group (Hazard Ratio 2.5).

key_claims.claim: The vast majority of ARIA-E cases are radiographically transient and asymptomatic.
key_claims.evidence: 98.2% of events resolved radiographically (82.8% within 16 weeks), and 74% of patients with ARIA-E remained asymptomatic.

key_claims.claim: ARIA-H (microhemorrhages and superficial siderosis) occurs more frequently in patients who also experience ARIA-E.
key_claims.evidence: Incidence of brain microhemorrhages was 40.3% in patients with ARIA-E versus 7.6% in those without ARIA-E in the 10-mg/kg group.

methods.design: Secondary analysis of two double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group, phase 3 randomized clinical trials
methods.population: Adults aged 50 to 85 years with mild cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer disease or mild Alzheimer disease dementia, with confirmed amyloid pathology

limitations: The trials were terminated early by the sponsor, leading to incomplete dosing courses for approximately 45% of the total participants, which could impact the long-term observation of adverse events.
The global phase 3 study populations lacked racial and ethnic diversity.
The study only evaluated patients with mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia; safety profiles in other disease stages remain unknown.
red_flags: The manuscript mentions in the Introduction that 'key assumptions on which the futility decision was based were not valid' to justify the subsequent analysis, which frames the early termination as a statistical error rather than a clinical failure, presenting a form of narrative spin in a safety paper.
The provided text lacks a conflict of interest or funding declaration section, which is critical given the controversial regulatory history of aducanumab.
